label: main:spectrum
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: main:star
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main:star}
Let $\mathcal U$ be a uniform ultrafilter on an infinite cardinal $\mu$, and let $2\leqslant r<\omega$. Every proper filter $\mathcal G\supseteq\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)}$ satisfies
\[
\chi(\mathcal G)\geqslant\chi(\mathcal U),\qquad
\chi(\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)})=\chi(\mathcal U).
\]
At the non-isolated point $p$ of the zero-dimensional Tychonoff space $Y=X(\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)})$,
\[
\pi\chi(p,Y)=\pi\chi_l(p,Y)=\mu,\qquad \pi\chi_c(p,Y)=\chi(\mathcal U).
\]
The stars form an $r$-linked local $\pi$-base of cardinality $\mu$. The space has cardinality $\mu$, and $p$ admits no decreasing local $\pi$-base.
head: environment

label: main:simultaneous
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main:simultaneous}
For every cardinal $\lambda>\omega_1$, there is a zero-dimensional Tychonoff space $X$ with
\[
\pi\chi(X)=\pi\chi_l(X)=\omega<\pi\chi_c(X)=\omega_1<\pi\chi_d(X)=\lambda
\]
such that, for every integer $r\geqslant2$, every point of this same space has a countable $r$-linked local $\pi$-base. One may have $|X|=\lambda$ and the optimal number of non-isolated points from Theorem~\ref{main:spectrum}, or instead choose $X$ crowded with the same cardinality.
head: environment

label: lem:traces
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:traces}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a free filter on $S$. A family $\mathcal B$ of non-empty open subsets of $X(\mathcal F)$ is a local $\pi$-base at $p$ if and only if its traces $\{B\cap S:B\in\mathcal B\}$ are coinitial in $\mathcal F$. Taking traces preserves linkedness, centeredness, every finite degree of linkedness, and inclusion chains. If $\mathcal B$ is a centered local $\pi$-base, every finite intersection of its traces is infinite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The first assertion follows directly from the basic neighborhoods $\{p\}\cup A$. Every non-empty finite intersection of open sets is open and therefore meets $S$, which proves preservation of the intersection properties; inclusion is also preserved. For the last assertion, consider a non-empty finite subfamily $\mathcal B_0\subseteq\mathcal B$. If each member contains $p$, its trace belongs to $\mathcal F$, so their intersection is infinite. Otherwise some member omits $p$. If the intersection of the traces were a finite set $a$, locality would provide $B_1\in\mathcal B$ contained in $\{p\}\cup(S\setminus a)$. Then the intersection of $\mathcal B_0\cup\{B_1\}$ would be empty, contradicting centeredness. The empty intersection is $S$, which is infinite.
head: environment

label: prop:extensions
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The traces of a centered local $\pi$-base generate a proper filter $\mathcal G$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:traces}. Coinitiality gives $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal G$. Closing a family of cardinality at most an infinite cardinal $\tau$ under finite intersections gives a base of cardinality at most $\tau$, so this proves one inequality. Conversely, a base for any proper filter $\mathcal G\supseteq\mathcal F$ is a centered family of non-empty open subsets of the discrete part $S$ and is coinitial in $\mathcal F$. It is therefore a centered local $\pi$-base at $p$.
head: environment

label: prop:chains
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:chains}
Every inclusion-chain local $\pi$-base at $p\in X$ has a coinitial subfamily which can be enumerated as a strictly decreasing transfinite sequence, of cardinality at most $\max\{\omega,|X|\}$ and no greater than the original family. Consequently, when $\pi\chi_d(p,X)$ is defined, it is either $\omega$ or a regular uncountable cardinal, and
\[
\pi\chi_d(p,X)\leqslant\max\{\omega,|X|\}.
\]
In particular, a countable space with $\pi\chi_c(p,X)>\omega$ admits no decreasing local $\pi$-base at $p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From a non-empty chain choose successively a member strictly contained in every previously chosen member, stopping as soon as the selected family is coinitial. The chain property makes the next choice possible whenever coinitiality fails. If $X$ is infinite, this recursion must stop before $|X|^+$: otherwise a point chosen from each successive difference would give $|X|^+$ distinct points of $X$. The finite case is immediate.

For regularity, suppose $\mu=\pi\chi_d(p,X)>\omega$. Refine a witnessing chain to a strictly decreasing sequence indexed by an ordinal $\theta$ with $|\theta|\leqslant\mu$. Minimality gives $|\theta|=\mu$. The ordinal $\theta$ is not a successor, since a last member would alone be a local $\pi$-base. Passing to a cofinal subsequence gives $\mu\leqslant\operatorname{cf}(\theta)\leqslant|\theta|=\mu$, so $\mu$ is regular. Finally, a chain of non-empty sets is centered.
head: environment

label: lem:finite
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $J\subseteq r$ of largest cardinality for which there are sets $A_j\in\mathcal U$, $j\in J$, such that
\[
a=S\setminus\bigcup_{j\in J}f_j^{-1}(A_j)
\]
is $\mathcal F$-positive. The empty choice is admissible. We have $J\ne r$: otherwise $A=\bigcap_{j<r}A_j\in\mathcal U$, and the filter member $\bigcup_{j<r}f_j^{-1}(A)$ would be disjoint from $a$.

Fix $i\notin J$. For every $A\in\mathcal U$, maximality says that $a\setminus f_i^{-1}(A)$ is not $\mathcal F$-positive. Thus some $B\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $B\cap a\subseteq f_i^{-1}(A)$, so $f_i^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal F_a$. The proper filter $(f_i)_*(\mathcal F_a)$ contains the ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ and therefore equals it. Equations~\eqref{eq:pushcharacter} and \eqref{eq:restrictcharacter} give the character bound.
head: environment

label: prop:uniform
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:uniform}
For every infinite cardinal $\mu$ there is a uniform ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $\mu$ with $\chi(\mathcal U)=2^\mu$. Every uniform ultrafilter on $\mu$ has character strictly greater than $\mu$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall the independent-family argument for the first assertion. Let
\[
\Omega=\{(s,H):s\in[\mu]^{<\omega},\ H\subseteq\mathcal P(s)\}.
\]
This set has cardinality $\mu$. For each $x\subseteq\mu$, put
\[
I_x=\{(s,H)\in\Omega:x\cap s\in H\}.
\]
The family $\mathcal I=\{I_x:x\subseteq\mu\}$ has cardinality $2^\mu$, and every finite Boolean combination of distinct members has cardinality $\mu$. Indeed, choose a finite $s_0$ distinguishing the finitely many sets $x$ involved. For each finite $s\supseteq s_0$, choose $H$ to realize the prescribed membership pattern. There are $\mu$ such sets $s$.

Generate a filter by all members of $\mathcal I$, all complements of subsets of $\Omega$ of cardinality less than $\mu$, and all sets
\[
\Omega\setminus\bigcap\mathcal J
\qquad(\mathcal J\in[\mathcal I]^\omega).
\]
Every finite intersection of generators has cardinality $\mu$. To verify this, for each of the finitely many countably infinite families $\mathcal J$ choose a member outside the finite list of positive generators. The Boolean combination making the positive generators true and the chosen members false has cardinality $\mu$; removing finitely many sets of cardinality less than $\mu$ preserves that cardinality. The Kuratowski--Zorn lemma extends this filter to an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, which is uniform.

If $\mathcal B$ were a base of $\mathcal U$ of cardinality $\tau<2^\mu$, choose $B_I\in\mathcal B$ with $B_I\subseteq I$ for each $I\in\mathcal I$. Some base member must be chosen for infinitely many distinct $I$: otherwise $2^\mu\leqslant\tau\cdot\omega<2^\mu$. Choose a countably infinite family $\mathcal J$ with that common base member $B$. Then $B\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal J$ while $\Omega\setminus\bigcap\mathcal J\in\mathcal U$, a contradiction. Identifying $\Omega$ with $\mu$ proves the first assertion.

For the second, suppose a uniform ultrafilter had a base $\{B_\alpha:\alpha<\mu\}$, repeating members if necessary. Recursively choose distinct points $x_\alpha,y_\alpha\in B_\alpha$ avoiding every earlier choice. At each stage fewer than $\mu$ points are excluded, even when $\mu$ is singular. The disjoint sets $\{x_\alpha:\alpha<\mu\}$ and $\{y_\alpha:\alpha<\mu\}$ both meet every base member. Both would therefore belong to the ultrafilter, which is impossible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $e\in E_r(\mu)$, let $f_i(e)$ be its $i$-th element in increasing order, $i<r$. Then
\[
H_A^{(r)}=\bigcup_{i<r}f_i^{-1}(A).
\]
If $\mathcal G\supseteq\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)}$ is proper, Lemma~\ref{lem:finite} gives $\chi(\mathcal U)\leqslant\chi(\mathcal G)$. If $\mathcal A$ is a base for $\mathcal U$, then $\{H_A^{(r)}:A\in\mathcal A\}$ is a base for $\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)}$. This proves the character assertions, and Proposition~\ref{prop:extensions} gives $\pi\chi_c(p,Y)=\chi(\mathcal U)$.

The stars give $\pi\chi_l(p,Y)\leqslant\mu$. Suppose $\mathcal P$ is a family of non-empty open sets with $|\mathcal P|<\mu$. Choose an edge $e_P\in P\cap E_r(\mu)$ for each $P\in\mathcal P$ and put $C=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}e_P$. Since $|C|<\mu$, the set $A=\mu\setminus C$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. The neighborhood $\{p\}\cup H_A^{(r)}$ contains none of the selected edges, and therefore contains no member of $\mathcal P$. Thus $\pi\chi(p,Y)\geqslant\mu$.

The space has cardinality $\mu$, whereas its centered local $\pi$-character is $\chi(\mathcal U)>\mu$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform}. Proposition~\ref{prop:chains} therefore excludes a decreasing local $\pi$-base at $p$.
head: environment

label: rem:original
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:original}
For $\mu=\omega$ and $r=2$, Kania defines his filter by requiring $\{n:L_n^{(2)}\subseteq B\}\in\mathcal U$. This is equivalent to \eqref{eq:starfilter}: in one direction take this set as $A$, and in the other use $A\subseteq\{n:L_n^{(2)}\subseteq B\}$. Theorem~\ref{main:star} computes the invariant of the original star space itself.
head: environment

label: cor:spectrum
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:spectrum}
For each fixed $r\geqslant2$, the possible centered local $\pi$-characters at the non-isolated points of the countable star spaces $X(\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)})$ are exactly $\operatorname{Sp}_\chi(\omega)$. Their minimum is $\mathfrak u$, and their maximum is $\mathfrak c$. In particular, Kania's lower estimate $\mathfrak p$ improves to $\mathfrak u$ for every defining free ultrafilter.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The exact spectrum and its extrema follow from Theorem~\ref{main:star}, the definition of $\mathfrak u$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform}. For completeness, $\mathfrak p\leqslant\mathfrak u$: a free ultrafilter base has the strong finite-intersection property and no infinite pseudointersection. If $P$ were such a pseudointersection, split it into two infinite pieces. One piece has complement in the ultrafilter, contradicting almost containment in that complement.
head: environment

label: cor:countable
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:countable}
For each infinite $\mu$ and fixed finite $r\geqslant2$, there is a zero-dimensional Tychonoff space $Y$ of cardinality $\mu$, with one non-isolated point, such that
\[
\pi\chi(Y)=\pi\chi_l(Y)=\mu,\qquad\pi\chi_c(Y)=2^\mu.
\]
Every point has an $r$-linked local $\pi$-base of cardinality at most $\mu$, and the non-isolated point has no decreasing local $\pi$-base.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Take a uniform ultrafilter on $\mu$ of character $2^\mu$ and apply Theorem~\ref{main:star}.
head: environment

label: prop:matrix
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:matrix}
The family $\mathcal G_{\kappa,\lambda}$ is a free filter. At the non-isolated point $q$ of $Z=X(\mathcal G_{\kappa,\lambda})$,
\[
\pi\chi(q,Z)=\pi\chi_l(q,Z)=\pi\chi_c(q,Z)=\kappa,
\qquad \pi\chi_d(q,Z)=\lambda.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every $G_e$ is non-empty: choose $\alpha$ above the second coordinates appearing in $e$. Also $G_e\cap G_f=G_{e\cup f}$. To omit finitely many $d_{\alpha_j,F_j}$, choose $\xi\in\kappa\setminus\bigcup_jF_j$ and $\beta\geqslant\alpha_j$ for every $j$. Then $G_{\{(\xi,\beta)\}}$ omits those points. This proves freeness.

For finite $F\subseteq\kappa$, let
\[
B_F=\{d_{\alpha,H}:F\subseteq H\}.
\]
These sets form a centered family of cardinality $\kappa$, and they are coinitial in $\mathcal G_{\kappa,\lambda}$: take $F$ to contain all first coordinates of a given finite $e$. Thus $\pi\chi_c(q,Z)\leqslant\kappa$.

Suppose $\mathcal P$ is a family of non-empty open sets with $|\mathcal P|<\kappa$. Choose $d_{\alpha_P,F_P}\in P\cap D$ for each $P\in\mathcal P$. Since $\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}F_P$ has cardinality less than $\kappa$, choose $\xi$ outside this union. Regularity of $\lambda$ gives $\beta<\lambda$ with $\beta\geqslant\alpha_P$ for all $P\in\mathcal P$. None of the chosen points belongs to $G_{\{(\xi,\beta)\}}$, so no member of $\mathcal P$ is contained in $\{q\}\cup G_{\{(\xi,\beta)\}}$. Hence $\pi\chi(q,Z)\geqslant\kappa$.

The sets
\[
C_\alpha=\{d_{\beta,F}:\beta\geqslant\alpha\}\qquad(\alpha<\lambda)
\]
form a decreasing coinitial family, so $\pi\chi_d(q,Z)\leqslant\lambda$. To prove the reverse inequality, let $\mathcal P$ be an inclusion-chain local $\pi$-base with $|\mathcal P|<\lambda$. For $P\in\mathcal P$, put
\[
T_P=P\cap D,\qquad K_P=\bigcap_{d\in T_P}d\subseteq S,
\qquad F_P^*=\{\xi<\kappa:\{\xi\}\times\lambda\subseteq K_P\}.
\]
All $T_P$ are non-empty. Each $F_P^*$ is finite, and the family of these sets is a chain, since $P\mapsto K_P$ reverses inclusion. A chain of finite sets has only countably many distinct members. Thus $\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}F_P^*$ is countable; since $\kappa>\omega$, choose $\xi$ outside it.

For each $P$, choose $d_{\alpha_P,F_P}\in T_P$ with $\xi\notin F_P$. Then
\[
K_P\cap(\{\xi\}\times\lambda)\subseteq\{\xi\}\times\alpha_P.
\]
Regularity of $\lambda$ gives $\beta=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\alpha_P<\lambda$, so $(\xi,\beta)$ belongs to no $K_P$. However, locality applied to $\{q\}\cup G_{\{s\}}$ for each $s\in S$ implies $S=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}K_P$. This contradiction proves the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:sum
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sum}
For a sum of two free filters, ordinary local $\pi$-character and centered local $\pi$-character are the minima of the respective component values. A decreasing local $\pi$-base exists in the sum exactly when it exists in a component, and its least infinite cardinality is the minimum over the components in which it exists. These conclusions extend to finite sums.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal B$ be a local $\pi$-base at the non-isolated point of $X(\mathcal F_0\oplus\mathcal F_1)$. For ordinary character, take the non-empty coordinate traces
\[
\mathcal P_i=\{B\cap S_i:B\in\mathcal B,\ B\cap S_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
If neither family were coinitial, choose $A_i\in\mathcal F_i$ containing no member of $\mathcal P_i$. Locality would give $B\subseteq\{p\}\cup A_0\cup A_1$. At least one trace is non-empty, contradicting the choice of $A_i$. Thus one coordinate supplies an ordinary local $\pi$-base of cardinality at most $|\mathcal B|$.

If $\mathcal B$ is centered, its traces on $S_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}S_1$ have the finite-intersection property. If both coordinate families failed that property, finitely many members witnessing failure in each coordinate would together contradict it. Hence one full coordinate family is centered and, by locality, coinitial in the corresponding filter. Projection also preserves chains. Conversely, a coinitial family in one component remains coinitial in the sum and retains each of the stated properties. Induction gives the finite-sum assertions.
head: environment

label: lem:ultra-linked
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ultra-linked}
Let $\mathcal U$ be a free ultrafilter on $S_0$ and $\mathcal F$ a free filter on a disjoint set $S_1$. Write $a=\pi\chi(p_1,X(\mathcal F))$ and $b=\pi\chi_l(p_1,X(\mathcal F))$. At the non-isolated point $p$ of $X(\mathcal U\oplus\mathcal F)$,
\[
\min\{\chi(\mathcal U),a\}\leqslant\pi\chi_l(p,X(\mathcal U\oplus\mathcal F))
\leqslant\min\{\chi(\mathcal U),b\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper bound uses a base of $\mathcal U$ or a linked local $\pi$-base in the second component. For the lower bound, suppose $\mathcal B$ is a linked local $\pi$-base of cardinality $\tau<\min\{\chi(\mathcal U),a\}$. Replace its members by their traces on $S_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}S_1$, using Lemma~\ref{lem:traces}. Since the non-empty $S_1$-traces have cardinality less than $a$, there is $A_1\in\mathcal F$ containing none of them. For each $A_0\in\mathcal U$, locality gives $B\in\mathcal B$ with $B\subseteq A_0\cup A_1$. Its $S_1$-trace is empty, so $B\subseteq A_0$.

It follows that $\mathcal B_0=\{B\in\mathcal B:B\subseteq S_0\}$ is linked and coinitial in $\mathcal U$. Every member of $\mathcal B_0$ belongs to $\mathcal U$: otherwise its complement belongs to $\mathcal U$, and coinitiality supplies a disjoint member of $\mathcal B_0$. Hence $\mathcal B_0$ is an actual base for $\mathcal U$, contradicting $\tau<\chi(\mathcal U)$.
head: environment

label: lem:ultra-space
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ultra-space}
If $\mathcal U$ is uniform on an infinite cardinal $\mu$, then at the non-isolated point of $X(\mathcal U)$ the ordinary local $\pi$-character is $\mu$, the linked and centered local $\pi$-characters are both $\chi(\mathcal U)$, and no decreasing local $\pi$-base exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Singletons give the ordinary upper bound. Choosing one point from each of fewer than $\mu$ proposed members and using the complement of those points in $\mathcal U$ proves the lower bound. A linked coinitial family consists of $\mathcal U$-positive sets and therefore of members of $\mathcal U$, so its cardinality is at least $\chi(\mathcal U)$. A base for $\mathcal U$ gives the matching centered upper bound. Finally, $\chi(\mathcal U)>\mu=|X(\mathcal U)|$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:chains} applies.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $\kappa\leqslant2^\mu$, and fix $r\geqslant2$. Suppose first that $\lambda$ is regular. Choose a uniform ultrafilter $\mathcal V$ on $\nu$ with $\chi(\mathcal V)=2^\nu$, and form on disjoint ground sets
\[
\mathcal F=\mathcal F_{\mathcal V}^{(r)}\oplus\mathcal G_{\kappa,\lambda}.
\]
At the non-isolated point of $X(\mathcal F)$, Theorem~\ref{main:star}, Proposition~\ref{prop:matrix} and Lemma~\ref{lem:sum} give
\[
\pi\chi=\pi\chi_l=\nu,\qquad\pi\chi_c=\min\{2^\nu,\kappa\}=\kappa,
\qquad\pi\chi_d=\lambda.
\]
Here the linked upper bound comes from the stars and the ordinary lower bound from the sum lemma. The stars also give an $r$-linked local $\pi$-base of cardinality $\nu$.

If $\mu=\nu$, take $X=X(\mathcal F)$. If $\mu<\nu$, choose a uniform ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $\mu$ with $\chi(\mathcal U)=2^\mu$ and set
\[
X=X(\mathcal U\oplus\mathcal F).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:sum} gives ordinary value $\mu$, centered value $\min\{2^\mu,\kappa\}=\kappa$, and decreasing value $\lambda$, since the ultrafilter component has no decreasing base. Lemma~\ref{lem:ultra-linked} gives linked value $\nu$, using $\nu<\kappa\leqslant2^\mu$. The stars in the $\mathcal V$-component retain their $r$-linked coinitial property. In both cases $X$ is zero-dimensional and Tychonoff, has cardinality $\lambda$, and has exactly one non-isolated point. All other points contribute only $\omega$ to the global invariants.

For singular $\lambda$, put $\delta=\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)$ and choose regular cardinals $\lambda_i$, $i<\delta$, such that
\[
\kappa<\lambda_i<\lambda,\qquad\sup_{i<\delta}\lambda_i=\lambda.
\]
They may be chosen as successor cardinals above a cofinal sequence; distinctness is not required. Let $X_i$ be the regular-case example with values $\mu,\nu,\kappa,\lambda_i$, and take the topological sum $X=\coprod_{i<\delta}X_i$. Local invariants are unchanged on passing to an open subspace containing the point: restrict a local $\pi$-base to members contained in that subspace, retaining locality and the intersection or inclusion properties; conversely, its open sets are open in the whole space. Therefore the global values are $\mu,\nu,\kappa,\lambda$, every point retains the required $r$-linked base, and
\[
|X|=\sum_{i<\delta}\lambda_i=\lambda,\qquad\operatorname{ni}(X)=\delta.
\]

Proposition~\ref{prop:chains} gives $\pi\chi_d(X)\leqslant\max\{\omega,|X|\}$ without any separation assumption, so $|X|\geqslant\lambda$ is necessary. At least one point is non-isolated. If $\lambda$ is singular, every pointwise decreasing local $\pi$-character is strictly below $\lambda$. Fewer than $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)$ non-isolated points would give a supremum below $\lambda$, since isolated points contribute only $\omega$. This proves the claimed optimality. The crowded assertion follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:crowded} below.

label: cor:onepoint
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:onepoint}
For infinite $\mu\leqslant\nu<\kappa<\lambda$, a Hausdorff space with exactly one non-isolated point and the values in \eqref{eq:target} exists if and only if $\kappa\leqslant2^\mu$ and $\lambda$ is regular.

title: Proof
body_md: Use Theorem~\ref{main:spectrum}, Carlson's bound, and pointwise regularity of the decreasing invariant.

title: Corollary

title: Proof

label: prop:simultaneous
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:simultaneous}
There is no countably based proper filter extending $\Sigma$. Consequently, at the non-isolated point of $X(\Sigma)$,
\[
\pi\chi=\pi\chi_l=\omega<\pi\chi_c,
\]
and no decreasing local $\pi$-base exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal G\supseteq\Sigma$ is proper with a countable base. If some $E_r$ is $\mathcal G$-positive, the trace on $E_r$ of $\mathcal G_{E_r}$ is a countably based proper filter extending $\mathcal F_\mathcal U^{(r)}$. Indeed, lift a member of that coordinate filter by taking full sets in the other coordinates. This contradicts Theorem~\ref{main:star}.

Otherwise $S\setminus E_r\in\mathcal G$ for every $r$. Every member of $\mathcal G$ then meets infinitely many coordinates, since the complements of any finitely many coordinates also belong to $\mathcal G$. Enumerate a base as $\{B_k:k<\omega\}$. Choose distinct $r_k\geqslant2$ and edges $e_k\in B_k\cap E_{r_k}$. Define $A\subseteq S$ by
\[
A\cap E_{r_k}=H_{\omega\setminus e_k}^{(r_k)}\quad(k<\omega),
\]
and let its other coordinate traces be the full coordinates. Each $e_k$ is finite, so $A\in\Sigma$. But $e_k\in B_k\setminus A$ for every $k$, contradicting the base property. Proposition~\ref{prop:extensions} now gives $\pi\chi_c>\omega$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:chains} excludes decreasing bases.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For regular $\lambda>\omega_1$, form $X(\Sigma\oplus\mathcal G_{\omega_1,\lambda})$. The coordinate stars give a countable $r$-linked local $\pi$-base for every finite $r$. The centered value is exactly $\omega_1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sum} and Proposition~\ref{prop:simultaneous}, and the decreasing value is $\lambda$. The space has size $\lambda$ and one non-isolated point. For singular $\lambda$, take a topological sum over $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)$ regular decreasing values cofinal in $\lambda$, as in Theorem~\ref{main:spectrum}. The same optimality argument applies. Proposition~\ref{prop:crowded} supplies the crowded versions.
head: environment

label: prop:crowded
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:crowded}
Let $\mathcal F$ be a free filter on an infinite set $S$. There is a crowded zero-dimensional Tychonoff space $Y$ of cardinality $|S|$, with a point $p$, such that all four local $\pi$-characters at $p$ agree with those at the non-isolated point of $X(\mathcal F)$, including existence of the decreasing invariant. The existence of an $r$-linked local $\pi$-base of any given infinite size bound is preserved for each finite $r$. At every other point of $Y$, all four invariants are $\omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Replace each $s\in S$ by a disjoint copy $\mathbb Q_s$ of the rationals, and adjoin $p$ with basic neighborhoods
\[
\{p\}\cup\bigcup_{s\in A}\mathbb Q_s\qquad(A\in\mathcal F).
\]
Each fiber is clopen, since $S\setminus\{s\}\in\mathcal F$, and each displayed neighborhood is clopen. The clopen bases of the rational fibers therefore give a clopen base for $Y$. The space is Hausdorff, hence zero-dimensional Tychonoff; it is crowded and has cardinality $|S|$.

For a non-empty open set $B\subseteq Y$, let
\[
\operatorname{supp}(B)=\{s\in S:B\cap\mathbb Q_s\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Every non-empty open set meets a fiber. The support map sends a local $\pi$-base at $p$ to a coinitial family in $\mathcal F$, preserves inclusions, and preserves each finite intersection property under consideration: a non-empty finite intersection is open and meets some fiber. Conversely, take traces of a local $\pi$-base in $X(\mathcal F)$ on $S$ and replace each trace $T$ by $\bigcup_{s\in T}\mathbb Q_s$. Lemma~\ref{lem:traces} and the definition of the neighborhoods show that locality and all the required properties are preserved. These two operations prove the equalities. Points inside the open rational fibers are first countable and have all four invariants equal to $\omega$.

title: Question
body_md: Suppose $\omega_1<\kappa\leqslant\mathfrak c$ and $\lambda>\kappa$ is regular. Is there a Hausdorff space with $\pi\chi=\pi\chi_l=\omega$, $\pi\chi_c=\kappa$, and $\pi\chi_d=\lambda$, such that every point has a countable $r$-linked local $\pi$-base for every finite $r$? Can this be achieved with one non-isolated point?

title: Question
body_md: Which of the tuples in Theorem~\ref{main:spectrum} can be realized by countably compact Hausdorff spaces? Which can be realized by compact Hausdorff spaces?
